items.summary: A proposed class action filed Nov 19 in Manhattan federal court alleges that Alibaba defrauded shareholders by knowingly understating export-control risks in its 2024, 2025 and 2026 annual reports, inflating its share price. The suit centers on Alibaba's relationship with Megaspeed, a Singaporean company suspected of helping Beijing access advanced Nvidia AI chips, whose executive Alice Huang had ties to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Shareholders say shares fell 14% over four days after media reports linking the spy scandal and tightening restrictions on Chinese AI companies' remote use of processors; one report attributed part of the decline to a Nov 12 Reuters article warning Washington could tighten such controls. The plaintiff, shareholder Withida Bihan, seeks unspecified damages for holders of Alibaba's American depositary shares between May 23, 2024 and Nov 11, 2026. CEO Eddie Wu is also named as a defendant; Nvidia faces separate lawsuits over the same scandal. Separately, on Nov 19 Wu said Alibaba remained on track for $100 billion (S$129 billion) in external cloud revenue and a 20% EBITDA margin by 2030 despite US curbs that could affect products and services from 2027. The article reports these claims as allegations in the lawsuit, not established facts; Alibaba did not immediately respond to comment requests.
items.title: Shareholders sue Alibaba over concealed ties to suspected spy in Nvidia scandal

items.summary: Anthropic's initial public offering went live on Wednesday with shares opening around $111 to $111.50, a 33% premium over the set IPO price of $83 per share. That price already exceeded the range Anthropic projected for itself ($70 to $78). The deal will raise more than $81 billion toward employees and company reserves; combined with prior fundraising and new private offerings timed around the public debut, analysts expect roughly $220 billion in cash on hand. An analyst quoted by TechCrunch said this would give Anthropic "more cash on hand than any company has ever had." At an opening price that implies a market cap over $2 trillion, Anthropic would rank above Meta, Tesla, and Walmart but below Apple, Amazon, Alphabet, Nvidia, and Microsoft. CEO Dario Amodei spoke before the bell about safety commitments rather than valuation.
items.title: Anthropic completes Nasdaq IPO at $83, shares trading 33% higher

items.summary: At Anthropic's Wall Street listing, described as the largest IPO in history, CEO Dario Amodei pledged before the Nasdaq opening bell that the company would pace AI development and remain under human control. He stated it unequivocally they "will not bend to either business nor political pressure." The commitment echoes a September plan for pacing AI advancement through safety coordination with other companies and third-party evaluators, which OpenAI's Sam Altman, Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis, and xAI's Elon Musk reportedly agreed with though few concrete commitments followed. Amodei framed risks from bad actors as avoidable rather than inevitable, citing alignment work and testing to keep systems under human control while claiming the IPO strengthens their resolve. Co-founder Daniela Amodei echoed safety commitment in a CNBC interview but characterized AI's promise as "incredible." The speech is attributed reporting; no concrete commitments beyond rhetorical pledges were made by other companies.
items.title: Anthropic CEO reaffirms AI safety commitments at Nasdaq debut

items.summary: Databricks announced that bulk migration of Tableau and Power BI dashboards to Databricks AI/BI is now generally available, extending the existing single-report /importBI workflow so one command can convert an entire folder of reports in a single run. Supported source formats are .twb, .twbx, .tds, .tdsx, .pbit, and .tmdl; files must be stored together in a directory within a Unity Catalog volume (dragging files into chat remains limited to one-off imports). The migration agent lists the reports it found, matches each workbook to its companion data source file where applicable, prompts for the destination catalog and schema, then queues and processes reports several at a time while reusing existing Unity Catalog tables and views. Each report runs as an independent background job with per-report status (Queued, Running, Completed), can be paused or halted from a chat status card, and each run is undoable; verification against the original source—optionally via read-only MCP connection rather than screenshots—is recommended before retiring any source report. The feature requires partner-powered AI features enabled at both account and workspace levels, and current limits on file count and size are defined in public /importBI documentation.
items.title: Databricks makes bulk dashboard migration generally available via Genie Code's /importBI skill

items.summary: Databricks announced a beta release of Genie Migrate for Serverless, an agent that automates migration of jobs and notebooks from classic to serverless compute. The tool runs via the /compute migrate command inside Genie on any job or notebook with no setup required, scanning workloads to mark their serverless readiness before proposing changes as reviewable diffs. Migration is reversible: nothing applies until a user approves it, though approving preserves the job's ID, schedule, and permissions. Bulk migration of jobs can run in the background via Databricks CLI version 1.24.0 or above using the compute-migrations command group; notebook bulk support is pending. The agent conservatively leaves uncertain Spark configs rather than removing them and performs only static validation today, with runtime Sandbox validation planned for later to compare migrated output against a classic baseline without affecting production tables. External sources of truth such as Databricks Asset Bundles jobs or Git-folder notebooks cannot yet be migrated. Bulk migration supports jobs but not notebooks; notebook support is coming soon.
items.title: Databricks launches Genie Migrate for Serverless in beta

items.summary: Chng Poh Hwa wrote to respond to a Nov 11 article about the Joo Chiat Shibuya-style scramble crossing trial, which begins on Nov 16. She welcomed the trial as an attempt to optimise traffic flow and enhance pedestrian safety but questioned whether authorities had considered how cyclists and personal mobility device users would use the new crossing. Because pedestrians move in all directions at a scramble crossing, she argued it is imperative that guidelines exist alongside strict enforcement action so accidents between riders and pedestrians are minimised.
items.title: Reader urges clear rules for cyclists and PMD users at Joo Chiat scramble crossing trial

items.summary: Reader K.B. Ryan Joshua Mahindapala wrote to The Straits Times in response to a Nov 12 report that the shopping centre formerly known as Wheelock Place was renamed Landmark Orchard following its acquisition by Hongkong Land for $1.1 billion. He argued that the name holds cultural significance for Singaporeans who grew up in the 1980s and 1990s, citing memories such as the Borders bookstore, which closed in 2011, and framed places like it as part of collective identity rather than purely commercial assets. Mahindapala acknowledged that property owners must refresh their assets to meet changing consumer expectations but requested that Hongkong Land preserve some recognition of the Wheelock Place name through a heritage feature or acknowledgement of the building's history.
items.title: Singaporean urges Hongkong Land to preserve Wheelock Place name

items.summary: Sarah Hanson-Young, Greens Senator for South Australia, contends that Big Tech is already building datacentres in Australia and that the current debate over copyright exceptions exists because Labor wants another incentive to secure their presence. She asserts that Australian music, publishing, journalism and art are being lobbied into unfettered access so AI companies can scrape copyrighted works without payment or permission, framing this as a threat to more than a century of copyright protections. Hanson-Young warns that any loopholes Australia creates would undermine protections worldwide, potentially making the country 'the Cayman Islands of AI' and a global pariah riddled with exceptions. She argues against an opt-out system in favour of laws guaranteeing consent, credit and compensation for creators. The piece is attributed to her as Greens Senator; it presents these positions as advocacy rather than established fact.
items.title: Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young argues Labor should not grant AI companies copyright loopholes to attract datacentres

items.summary: Claire Vo, who runs ChatPRD—an AI platform for product managers to turn ideas into specs—reports a surge of token fraud from groups abusing the product's free trial. The abuse includes using tokens merely for free usage and tunneling through the agent to resell tokens or run commercial operations; one example involved prompts generating SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles, which may help scammers fingerprint underlying model families by their output signatures. ChatPRD has been live since the GPT-4 era, with Vo building it in public for much of that time. In response, she is winding down free trials entirely, a move presented as appropriate given the abuse but noted to have negative consequences.
items.title: ChatPRD ends free trials amid token fraud

items.summary: The Dutch data protection authority, Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), advised people not to buy AI-enabled smart glasses available on the Dutch market, following tests of six unnamed devices that ranged in price from under €100 (£84) to over €500 and came from different continents. The AP reported that during testing one pair repeatedly told a user an ambulance was en route when emergency services had not actually been contacted; another gave dating advice to an adult who expressed romantic interest in a minor, while others misread medicine packaging instructions and severe weather warnings. Beyond AI reliability, the authority flagged privacy risks including secret filming with obscured recording lights that some manufacturers claimed would disable the device but still functioned, security flaws allowing nearby users to connect without permission or operate cameras remotely, and data often exported outside the EU. The AP stopped short of calling for a ban on sale; it said its investigation focused mainly on algorithms and AI rather than data protection, though broader concerns about non-consensual filming remain. Meta recently released glasses without a camera amid privacy backlash, but whether they were tested is unknown, as was whether any of the three manufacturers approached by the BBC (Meta, TCL, HTC) had products in the test set.
items.title: Dutch privacy watchdog advises against buying AI smart glasses after testing six models

items.summary: The Senate passed the Bipartisan Affordability and American Jobs Act (BAAJA) on Thursday by a 62-33 vote, speeding up federal environmental permits for clean energy projects, transmission lines, gas pipelines, and data centers. The passage split the climate movement: nearly every member of the Environment and Public Works Committee voted against it except lead negotiator Sheldon Whitehouse, while Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto also voted no over narrowed Tribes' consultation rights; changes in recent weeks nonetheless won utility lobbying group Edison Electric Institute and Evergreen Action's support. The bill now goes to the House, where more than 100 moderate Democrats are warming to it but Reps. Jared Huffman and Rashida Tlaib oppose it, arguing for waiting until next year when Democrats control Congress. Supporters frame BAAJA as their best shot given President Trump has two years left in office and would likely veto a Democratic version; Sen. Lisa Murkowski said during floor debate, "This is our best option, not only for now, but likely for years to come." The bill sets faster agency review timelines, shortens the window to sue from years to 150 days, makes it harder for courts to block projects under the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act, and Endangered Species Act (allowing construction even if a federal environmental review is ruled deficient), narrows state and Tribes' authority to deny projects over water pollution, gives the government greater power to approve transmission when states delay them, softens an initial provision that would have eliminated utilities' right of first refusal for grid upgrades, and includes "permit certainty" provisions banning administrations from vacating issued permits except in emergencies or under new laws. A Rhodium Group forecast attributes a 1% to 18% reduction in power sector emissions by 2040 (depending on clean energy's price competitiveness with gas) and $50 to $78 lower average annual household electricity bills, though it excludes behind-the-meter data center gas plants; these are forecasts, not established outcomes. Trump endorsed the bill via Truth Social, and a White House ratepayer protection pledge would effectively double charges for data centers' new transmission lines and existing grid use, with implementation left to FERC.
items.title: Senate passes bipartisan permitting reform bill in 62-33 vote

items.summary: Marathon Petroleum's Martinez Renewables facility northeast of San Francisco was cited by California's Cal/OSHA for 10 violations, three classified as serious: inadequate training, uninsulated high-temperature equipment and faulty emergency eyewash stations. The citations followed a strike that turned into a June lockout after Marathon rejected the union's unconditional return-to-work offer during contract negotiations over fatigue from chronic understaffing and overtime shifts. Workers reported frequent intense flaring with 20-foot flames once they left their April 27 shift, prompting United Steelworkers Local 5 president Nick Plurkowski to call Cal/OSHA the next day; inspectors found at least a dozen employees untrained, including two shift supervisors and 10 operators. The violations echo findings from the U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board's March 2025 report on the November 2022 explosion that killed operator Jerome Serrano during the plant's transition to renewable fuels, which attributed the incident to inadequate operating procedures, burner training and engineering controls. Marathon spokesperson Jamal Kheiry said Martinez Renewables has appealed the citations and disputed them by stating it continues staffing the facility with qualified personnel; a Cal/OSHA spokesperson confirmed the appeal and declined further comment pending resolution. Negotiations are scheduled to resume Dec. 1 with federal mediation support, though Plurkowski doubted good faith after six months of lockout.
items.title: California fined Marathon over safety violations at Martinez Renewables refinery amid worker lockout

items.summary: ExxonMobil announced that total Guyana oil production topped 1 million barrels per day, a milestone reached seven years after first oil in 2019. The Stabroek Block, developed by Exxon along with partners Hess and CNOOC since the company acquired it in 1999, yielded discoveries estimated at over 11 billion barrels of crude; these figures are reported claims rather than verified totals. Rystad Energy analyst Schreiner Parker told the Financial Times that Guyana was a textbook example of right place, right time and became one of ExxonMobil's crown jewels in its repositioning, with development speed from first oil to over 1 million barrels per day described as seemingly achievable only by ExxonMobil; these are attributed opinions. The article frames this success against the green investment movement that pushed exploration aside after the Paris Agreement, arguing forecasts of near-term peak oil demand have not materialized and that European Union oil and gas imports did not slump during a Middle East supply disruption but moved slightly lower while rising in value because of price shocks; these are claims rather than established facts. The piece asserts that other Big Oil majors are now returning to frontier regions for production boosts instead of divesting assets into solar and battery businesses, citing South America (Suriname, Brazil, Argentina), a Venezuela back on the map after U.S. involvement in its oil industry, Africa, and Asia as destinations; these are reported plans rather than outcomes.
items.title: Guyana's oil boom rekindles frontier drilling among major oil companies

items.summary: Swedish advanced nuclear developer Blykalla signed an agreement on Nov. 12, announced Nov. 16, that the companies describe as the world's first high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) enrichment contract for a commercial lead-cooled reactor. The deal covers Blykalla's first commercial SEALER unit, its 55-MWe Swedish Advanced Lead Reactor planned for U.S. deployment; under it, Blykalla supplies the uranium feed and Urenco enriches material at its Capenhurst facility in England, which is expected online by 2031 with deliveries to begin in the early 2030s. Neither company disclosed the contract value or enrichment level for SEALER fuel; Stedman said only that it secures HALEU enrichment for "at least our first commercial unit." The agreement covers just the enrichment stage, not finished-fuel supply, which Blykalla has not identified and is developing through an integrated sourcing strategy. This is Urenco's third HALEU contract after Radiant (Sept. 2025) and Antares Nuclear (May 2026). The DOE defines HALEU as uranium enriched above 5% but below 20%, versus up to 5% for typical commercial reactor fuel, and has projected domestic demand could reach 50 metric tons annually by 2035. Urenco received £196 million in May 2024 under a program committing up to £300 million; the Capenhurst facility totals roughly £400 million with an initial capacity of up to 27 metric tons of HALEU annually, designed for future expansion.
items.title: Blykalla signs world's first HALEU enrichment contract for a commercial lead-cooled reactor with Urenco.

items.summary: Analysts note that crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf have rebounded near pre-war levels, while Brent slid to about $92 per barrel from a late-October peak above $118. The market and most analysts assume steady Middle Eastern flows will continue into next year and eventually produce an oil surplus; investment banks and the IEA expect that surplus as early as this quarter, with Goldman Sachs projecting Brent averaging $88 in 2027 under its base case of no diplomatic breakthrough. However, inbound tanker traffic to Hormuz is at risk: since late August, empty-tanker capacity bound for the Gulf of Oman fell roughly 40%, and combined ballasting supertanker and Suezmax capacity there dropped from 130 million barrels on Aug. 31 to 71 million as of Nov. 16, per Tankertrackers.com cited by Bloomberg; co-founder Samir Madani said "not enough vacant tankers" exist to take oil out of the region. Meanwhile tanker attacks intensified—five vessels were struck near Hormuz between Nov. 11 and 18, per Windward—and IEA and Goldman both flag that shipping-attack risks undermine their surplus forecasts.
items.title: Tanker Shortage Threatens Hormuz Oil Exports Despite Recovery

items.summary: Japanese and South Korean equities plunged in early trade on November 20 as chip-related stocks declined following a rough session on Wall Street. The Nikkei 225 was down 4.02 per cent at 57,051.43 points, while the Kospi fell 3.81 per cent to 4,942.22 points. These moves came even though Anthropic's initial public offering raised a record US$81.3 billion and its shares closed 17 per cent higher in their Nasdaq debut on Thursday; that gain occurred amid broader weakness with the tech-heavy Nasdaq and S&P 500 each closing down more than 2 per cent. Online brokerage Monex noted that strong demand for Anthropic stock led some to suggest a possible shift of funds away from high-tech stocks toward the newly listed company's shares, but this did not settle market nerves amid ongoing fallout from Nvidia's crisis.
items.title: Asian stock indices fell sharply on Friday after chip stocks dropped on Wall Street, despite Anthropic's record IPO

items.summary: Anthropic became the first major AI lab to go public, raising US$81 billion in an offering of 980 million shares priced at US$83 each on Nov 19, surpassing SpaceX's prior record of about US$75 billion and SK Hynix's US$26.5 billion and Aramco's US$25.6 billion. The initial $1.5 trillion valuation rose to roughly US$2.01 trillion when shares opened at US$111.50, then settled near US$97.17 per share for a market value of about US$1.75 trillion by close. Anthropic joined SpaceX as the second company ever to debut above $1 trillion and became one of 13 companies in that tier overall; Apple leads the S&P 500 at US$5.1 trillion, ahead of Microsoft (US$3.8 trillion) and Nvidia (US$3.6 trillion). The article notes Anthropic proceeded despite investor jitters over volatility, AI-bubble fears, and public unease about the technology's risks; it also frames $1 trillion as roughly 156 million km laid end to end or nearly US$122 per person globally.
items.title: Anthropic's IPO raised a record $81 billion at a $1.5 trillion valuation

items.summary: Anthropic completed what its announcement describes as the largest initial public offering on record, with Nasdaq reporting a valuation of $1.8 trillion at the debut. CEO Dario Amodei stated that the listing strengthens the company's financial position while reinforcing its commitment to prioritizing safety over commercial or political demands; he said Anthropic will pace AI training and deployment as long as necessary for confidence in safety and human control, adding it would not bend to either business or political pressure.
items.title: Anthropic completes record IPO as Amodei vows AI safety over commercial and political pressure

items.summary: On November 19, California Attorney General Rob Bonta served Nvidia with an investigative subpoena probing whether its advanced semiconductors reached China in violation of US export rules and whether the company misled investors. The probe reportedly followed one week after former CEO Jensen Huang resigned amid allegations involving multiple extramarital affairs, including a relationship with Alice Huang, who is not related to him and was described as a suspected Chinese spy. She had been an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based firm under investigation for allegedly diverting restricted Nvidia chips to China. The subpoena asserts these events occurred but does not establish them; the allegations remain unverified claims rather than confirmed facts.
items.title: California AG subpoenas Nvidia over alleged China chip diversion and investor disclosures

items.summary: Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston told Semafor that his proposed $115 billion all-stock merger with chipmaker Marvell has been unpopular, describing it as 'a rough go.' The deal combines Lumentum's optical technology business into Marvell's chips businesses. Shares in both companies fell roughly 40% since the announcement on April 23 over concerns about AI trade runway and claims that Lumentum sold too soon. Hurlston said he expects shares to rebound as more information reaches analysts, while acknowledging a material adverse change clause exists but noting its exercise conditions are limited. He cited an 80% overlap in shareholder bases between the two companies as a source of forced selling among portfolio managers holding one stock but not the other. The merger faces regulatory review in both the US and China, with scrutiny heightened by the Nvidia chip scandal; Hurlston said he and Marvell CEO Matt Murphy have previously navigated SAMR approvals. Separately, Semafor reported that Murphy could be considered for Nvidia's CEO role after Jensen Huang's resignation, a possibility Hurlston acknowledged without confirming.
items.title: Lumentum's CEO defends $115 billion all-stock deal with Marvell amid investor backlash

items.summary: Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto VI is expected to surpass $3 billion in its first week, a figure that would eclipse the lifetime grosses of some major films and concert tours. The Economist argues this windfall coincides with industry mass layoffs, suggesting developers face shrinking incentives to create comparable titles as hardware costs rise and generative AI pushes smaller teams toward lower-spec games; these are presented as arguments rather than established outcomes. The New York Times Magazine reviewed the game favorably, praising it as a satisfying simulacrum of American life amid claims that the United States resembles one of its settings.
items.title: Grand Theft Auto VI projected to exceed $3 billion in first-week sales

items.summary: Anthropic opened its Nasdaq debut on November 19 with a fully diluted valuation of about $2 trillion, surpassing SpaceX's June listing. Shares rose from an $83 Wednesday IPO price to $111.50 before ending Thursday at $97.17, up 17% over the offering price; based on outstanding shares alone, market value peaked near $1.5 trillion. The company sold 980 million shares above its initial range of $70-$78, with proceeds potentially reaching $93.5 billion if underwriters fully exercise their option, though they currently stand at over $107 billion including a separate private placement in which AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC invested an additional $26 billion. The debut occurred as AI enthusiasm cooled amid questions about whether high valuations and heavy computing spending can yield sustainable profits; the company's net loss narrowed while revenue rose 4% quarter-on-quarter despite slowing growth, with nearly $900 billion in computing commitments to partners including Amazon and Alphabet's Google. Analysts offered caution: Bob O'Donnell of TECHnalysis Research called it a reassuring step but said stability still depends on OpenAI, Nvidia and data-center policy; Talley Leger of The Wealth Consulting Group advised against buying high-profile tech IPOs at first-day prices, citing historical underperformance versus broader indexes over three years. CEO Dario Amodei told CNBC the company hopes to reach investment-grade credit status eventually.
items.title: Anthropic's Nasdaq IPO valued at roughly $2 trillion, edging past SpaceX

items.summary: The Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, held in Shenzhen under the theme "To Prosper and Win the Future Together," opened on 15 November 2025. Chinese President Xi Jinping was to deliver the keynote speech at a forum whose stated focus is cooperation rather than competition. China and the United States agreed to pause their reciprocal tariffs until early January while trade talks proceed, though the arrangement leaves disputes unresolved as the meeting began.
items.title: APEC meeting opens with US-China tariffs paused until early January

items.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham asked social media companies to take down a YouTube video in which convicted rapist Russell Brand protested his innocence, saying victims "shouldn't be hearing from him." The account was read by his wife Laura and uploaded on Sunday after Brand received 10.5 years for one rape count and three sexual assault counts against four women; police are investigating additional allegations. UK government minister Matthew Pennycook told the BBC that authorities have no power to force content removal, describing it as "up to Google," while a ministry spokesman said YouTube should remove the video but noted removal depends on platform terms. The account has more than 6.6 million subscribers and the video reportedly exceeded 950,000 views; Brand's Facebook and Instagram accounts appear unavailable, his monetising program was suspended in September 2023, and his X account with 10 million followers remains visible but inactive since November 11. As of Friday at 10am AEST the video remained online after Google reportedly refused on the basis that its rules had not been broken; UK officials are investigating whether Brand violated laws barring prisoners from broadcasting messages or posting to social media, noting inmates cannot circumvent these rules by having others publish their comments. Burnham declined to commit to changing the law, saying "I wouldn't leap to that."
items.title: UK government urges Google to remove Russell Brand's innocence video; request reportedly refused

items.summary: The 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting adopted an APEC Connectivity Blueprint on Thursday, per a report noting the document's adoption. The meeting took place in Shenzhen, where an APEC-themed floral installation was displayed at the Qianhai International Convention Center on October 23, 2026. No further details about the blueprint's contents or commitments are provided.
items.title: APEC leaders adopt connectivity blueprint at 33rd Economic Leaders' Meeting

items.summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping met Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on Friday in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province. The city hosted the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting from Wednesday to Thursday.
items.title: Xi meets Albanese in Shenzhen during APEC meeting

items.summary: Following recent convictions and allegations against older men, including claims by two women against Russell Brand and David Walliams, a campaign is pushing to close the UK's 'consent gap.' The proposal would set an age of consent at 16 but restrict sex between 16- or 17-year-olds with partners more than three years their senior. The government is reportedly seriously considering this staggered approach. Nosheen Iqbal spoke with Guardian columnist Polly Hudson about why culture and law have left girls vulnerable to exploitation by older men, and educator Michael Conroy explained what he believes must be done for change to occur.
items.title: UK government considering staggered age of consent law

items.summary: For the second time in four years, Formula One returned to Las Vegas for a race whose World Drivers' and Constructors' Championships had already been settled. Mercedes secured its estimated $140 million constructors' title payout by winning at Sao Paulo earlier this month, following Kimi Antonelli's drivers' championship win in Mexico City. Although the championships were decided, teams still compete for remaining prize-money positions: second place earns an estimated $131 million and third place an estimated $122 million, with further payouts continuing down the standings.
items.title: Formula One Las Vegas Grand Prix held after championships decided, with prize money still at stake

items.summary: Japan Tobacco will record a ¥1.4 trillion ($8.9 billion) charge after Russian presidential decrees placed all seven of its local subsidiaries under temporary administration, causing the company to lose management control and remove them from consolidated accounts. The write-down pushes the cigarette maker into a full-year net loss: it now expects an operating loss of ¥368 billion instead of a ¥1 trillion profit, with revenue cut by ¥63 billion to ¥3.8 trillion as its dividend forecast is slashed. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi raised asset seizures and Russia's arrest of a Japanese journalist during her meeting with Vladimir Putin in China on Wednesday.
items.title: Japan Tobacco takes $8.9 billion charge after Russia seizure of subsidiaries

items.summary: At Berlin's Coalition of the Willing summit, European leaders said they were prepared to negotiate with Russia over ending the war in Ukraine. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham described Europe's negotiating position as clear and united; German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's maximalist demands are not realistic and rejected any division of Europe into major-power spheres of influence, calling a 'Yalta format' peace unacceptable. Jared Kushner said Trump wanted to make a deal with Moscow 'with Europe by his side,' while Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led talks but claimed Russia was not against it pending clarification of what Europe would bring. Zelensky and Merz were more sceptical than Kushner, noting that Putin had spurned every proposal so far; Macron urged allies to deliver air defence systems and reopen Ukraine's Nato membership question. The article notes mixed signals from Moscow: US envoys Witkoff and Kushner appeared confident of a European seat last week, while aide Yury Ushakov this week said much more must be done before four-sided talks could occur. It also reports that Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, continues attacking Kyiv's energy infrastructure as winter approaches with rising civilian casualties and no movement on territorial demands, and struck several buildings in central Kyiv during the summit, killing one person; Putin vowed a 'considerably more painful' response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge. The article frames these statements as claims or plans rather than established outcomes: readiness for talks is reported but not confirmed, Moscow's position remains mixed, and no peace agreement has been reached.
items.title: European leaders say they are ready for talks with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine

items.summary: A 57-year-old man from Cook was killed Thursday afternoon in a collision with a red Kia Cerato driven by a 19-year-old woman from Sutton, NSW, near Horse Park Drive and the Federal Highway. The driver tested negative for alcohol and is not believed to have been speeding; witnesses gave first aid before paramedics arrived but the cyclist could not be revived. This was Canberra's 13th road fatality this year and its third cyclist death in recent months, following August deaths of Bridie Lee (32) and Ryan Riethmuller (39), struck by a car on Gungahlin Drive whose driver Thi Phuong Ngoc Nguyen has pleaded not guilty to two counts of culpable driving causing death and one count of negligent driving occasioning actual bodily harm. Detective Inspector Mark Steel told 666 ABC Radio Canberra that vulnerable road users made up the majority of fatalities this year, describing cycling on roads as "a game of Russian roulette" unless motorists are mindful; these statements represent his opinion rather than established fact. The Vikings Cycling Club and Canberra Cycling Club posted tributes offering support services to members.
items.title: Cyclist killed on Canberra Federal Highway; third cyclist fatality this year

items.summary: As American voters passed 40 of 41 ballot initiatives limiting or preventing data centre development in this month's midterms, Canadian industry leaders are treating the retreat as an opportunity. Lucy Hargreaves, CEO of Build Canada, said on X that "data centres in Canada looking pretty appealing right now," and told the BBC some US-bound capital is becoming available for Canada. Proponents argue abundant land, natural gas, and cold climate let Canada address US problems like proximity to populated areas, noise pollution, and grid strain. Pushback has been muted so far: most projects proceed without major disruption, and legislators have embraced them with little political cost. Alberta anchors the boom, hosting 90% of proposed sites and pitching itself as "North America's destination of choice" via a concierge investor service; Kevin O'Leary announced two Wonder Valley sites (one in Alberta, one in Utah), while Meta is building a C$13bn ($9bn; £6.8bn) centre in the province. The Alberta project would be 7,000 acres and 7.5 gigawatts, billed as off-grid on regional natural gas, was exempted from an environmental impact assessment in April (still needing permits), drew limited opposition at a town hall, and is projected to use six million cubic metres of water annually—about the size of 2,400 Olympic-size pools. Paul Palandjian oversees both O'Leary projects and said they are proceeding at "equal" pace; he acknowledged it had become more of a hot topic in the US than Alberta, though public anger there is growing. Signs of resistance include furious residents at August town halls after Alberta announced Meta's centre, Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation suing over the environmental override for Wonder Valley (calling it irrational), and hundreds protesting an Anthropic data centre in Nova Scotia. Sean Mullin, a University of Toronto senior fellow and former adviser to Canada's prime minister on sovereign AI compute strategy, said "AI is generally not very popular" in both countries and warned Canada could face similar backlashes if unthoughtful; he attributed the milder Canadian reaction partly to scope and timing—fewer projects attracting less attention. The Carney government has framed development as national security and sovereignty, projecting a 16-fold expansion of computing capacity over four years, while Ontario's Doug Ford said his province must move "full steam ahead." High-level guidance co-signed by Anthropic, Meta, and others calls on centres to pay for electricity, minimise water use, and create long-term regional benefits. Bek MacIntosh, an Alberta resident who halted a data centre in Olds over scale, scope, and proximity, fears reckless developers could trigger angry votes like those seen in the US if provinces do not develop responsibly; she said no political party appears prepared for it.
items.title: Canada courts US investors retreating from AI data centres amid muted local pushback

items.summary: Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez acknowledged his government had made "mistakes" but insisted it has always governed in the right direction, opening Thursday's campaign-deciding televised debate against conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo. The two clashed over the economy, housing, immigration, corruption and foreign policy amid a November 29 election that could bring far-right Vox into government if no majority forms. Sánchez cited economic growth and employment figures to argue Spain is in better shape than when he took power in 2018; Feijóo rejected this, accusing the government of crushing the middle class while families struggle with soaring prices and a housing crisis. Polls show Socialists trailing PP, which is predicted to win most seats without a majority, leaving Vox as decisive third force after it governed regionally with PP in 2023; Sánchez's weakened left-wing coalition partners further complicate his position. Feijóo blamed the government for two high-speed train collisions that killed 115 people and called Sánchez unfit to lead, while Sánchez warned a PP-Vox coalition would roll back social rights and defended Spain's liberal immigration approach against European trends toward stricter controls.
items.title: Sánchez admits mistakes in Spain's only televised debate before election

items.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron called on Ukraine's allies at a Berlin 'Coalition of the Willing' summit, co-hosted with Germany and the UK, to speed up delivery of air defence systems and "reopen the question" of Ukraine's accession to NATO. He framed this as necessary given what he described as Russia's maximalist position, prioritising deployment of anti-missile systems and interceptors. The summit drew more than 25 leaders alongside President Volodymyr Zelensky, taking place hours after a three-way US-Russia-China summit in Shenzhen where Trump, Putin and Xi reportedly agreed a peace declaration that Macron said does not reorganise the world. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz expected new Ukraine peace talks soon on neutral ground, naming the United Arab Emirates as a possible location without giving a date; British Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged continued support for Ukraine. US envoy Jared Kushner reported Trump supported European involvement in any deal and was open to extending an Article Five-like security guarantee to Ukraine if it served American interests, while Zelensky said a real guarantee would require US or European forces and bases on Ukrainian territory.
items.title: Macron urges allies to reopen Ukraine's NATO membership question

items.summary: Nobel economist Joseph Stiglitz said recent youth protests across Europe are "legitimate" complaints, attributing them to intergenerational inequality in which young people cannot afford housing or adequate education. Hundreds of thousands protested in France, Denmark, Italy and Spain over rising living costs, a housing crisis and poor pay; the article reports these figures as reported events rather than Stiglitz's own claims. In Spain, protesters held a nationwide 24-hour strike for the first time since 2012 amid reports that some rent €460 a month for a five-square-metre bedroom in Barcelona, though this is presented as an individual account rather than a general statistic. Stiglitz said "part of the problem [...] is inequality across generations" and warned that rising inequality, climate change and AI-related anxieties create uncertainty for younger people who may never match their parents' living standards; these are his characterizations, not established facts about future outcomes. He endorsed taxing the ultra-wealthy as a way to fund public services, citing French economist Gabriel Zucman's proposal of roughly two per cent on fortunes above €100 million and arguing such taxes should be levied at EU level because free movement makes tax avoidance easier; this is Stiglitz advocating a specific proposal rather than it being established policy. He cautioned that taxation alone would not resolve Europe's challenges, recommending public spending reform and more flexible pension systems to reflect longer life expectancy and physically demanding jobs.
items.title: Joseph Stiglitz backs European youth protests as legitimate and calls for taxing the ultra-wealthy

items.summary: A jury at Winchester Crown Court found four British men guilty on Thursday of multiple sexual offences, including rape, against Joanne Young, 49, whose then-husband Philip Young had drugged her and advertised her for sex online. Police uncovered hundreds of intimate images after investigating Mr Young in 2024 over uploading bestiality imagery, exposing a wider pattern of abuse; he filmed her without consent at their Swindon home. The four men, aged between 32 and 62, were convicted after being recruited online: Norman Macksoni (48) was found guilty of rape; Richard Wilkins (62) of rape and assault by penetration; Connor Sanderson-Doyle (32) of assault by penetration and sexual touching; Mohammed Hassan of sexual touching. Mr Young had earlier pleaded guilty to dozens of offences, including 11 counts of rape and 11 counts of administering a substance with intent. A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton (47), admitted one count of assault by penetration, two counts of sexual assault and one count of rape. Justice Pushpinder Saini said the four men faced significant prison sentences and praised Ms Young's bravery. She waived her anonymity, expressed relief at the verdicts, urged other victims to come forward saying they "can be believed and understood," and described how the abuse had cost her life as she knew it. The case was likened by reporting to that of Gisèle Pelicot in France.
items.title: Four British men convicted of raping a woman drugged and advertised by husband

items.summary: An expert on U.S.-China relations at Harvard Kennedy School assessed the Nov. 19, 2026 trilateral meeting of Trump, Putin and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, held during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, arguing it delivered more style than substance. The author attributes this to heavy symbolism: Xi greeting Trump at the airport (a special honor) and an unprecedented hug between them were choreographed displays; seating Xi centrally framed China as a steadying 'Middle Kingdom,' which the writer notes reflects how Xi wants Beijing seen rather than its actual global presence. On policy, all three agreed reforming the U.N. is needed with China seeking more power while Trump grows disillusioned, and they signed a document on nuclear controls built around Reagan-Gorbachev's 1985 phrase 'Nuclear war cannot be won, must never be fought,' though it contained few commitments given expired treaties and Beijing lagging in capacity; the author flags that Beijing may hold different views. The writer asserts the wars in Iran (ongoing roughly nine months) and Ukraine were not discussed substantively—Ukraine by name at all—with speculation that China or Russia could have helped pressure Iran but neither was willing to offer assistance, while Europe's absence made a Trump-Ukraine statement impractical; AI regulation and critical mineral supply chains are said not to have been raised publicly though possibly in bilateral talks. Comparing it to the 1945 Yalta Conference, the author notes differences: Britain was part of that 'big three' but China is absent now, and Stalin-Roosevelt-Churchill were comrades-in-arms who later drifted apart as the Cold War began, whereas here China and Russia are partners with the U.S. seen as their adversary; the writer speculates Trump may want détente rather than a new Cold War and questions whether Europe will object to such an emerging order.
items.title: Harvard Kennedy School expert characterizes Xi-Putin-Trump Shenzhen summit as symbolic with little policy substance

items.summary: Olivia Cheung, welcomed by Genie Godula, describes the Xi Jinping-Trump-Putin trilateral meeting at the APEC summit as significant despite lacking concrete agreements. She attributes its importance to what she calls "the precedence of the United States seeing and giving recognition that China and Russia are peers of the United States," arguing that this framing produces a notable image of a G3, though these assessments remain Cheung's interpretation rather than established outcomes or commitments from the meeting itself.
items.title: Olivia Cheung characterizes Trump's framing of China and Russia as US 'peers' at a trilateral APEC meeting.

items.summary: Experts attribute rising human-wildlife conflict in Sri Lanka to habitat fragmentation from deforestation, food-search behavior by displaced species, improved road connectivity via expressways, and a decline in predators. Peacocks have spread from the dry zone into Colombo's wet-zone suburbs since 2020; Sarath Kotagama links this partly to people altering vegetation and temperature conditions enabling movement across cleared strips such as those beside the Southern Expressway (about 300 meters of open habitat). Primatologist Charmalie Nahallage says purple-faced leaf langurs, forced onto rooftops by fragmented forest, become pests when fed or given access to dumped food waste. Ceylon spotted deer in Homagama number roughly 1,500-2,500 and are increasingly hit on roads; the Department of Wildlife Conservation has successfully translocated recovered animals to Udawalawe National Park (about 118 kilometers southeast of Colombo). At Attidiya center, wildlife veterinarian Pramuditha Devasurendra reported that in 2025 there were 4,855 cases total: 1,822 mammals, 1,879 birds and 1,154 reptiles and other species; recoveries totaled 643 mammals, 675 birds and 848 reptiles (2,167 animals released). He said about 80% of cases involve electrocution or road accidents, air rifle attacks on monkeys have risen since 2018, and recovery rates are roughly 70% for serpents/reptiles versus 20-25% for monkeys. Hasini Sarathchandra (DWC) noted peacock numbers may spike because jackals that ate their eggs have declined; Nahallage added that urban rattlesnakes feeding on the same prey are now rarely seen, illustrating disrupted food webs. Kotagama argues coexistence requires people to accept these animals as non-pests rather than targets of air rifles and electrocution.
items.title: Sri Lankan wild animals increasingly move into cities as habitat is fragmented and predators decline

items.summary: The European Union, via a statement from the European Commission's diplomatic service on 20 November 2026, urged Myanmar to fully and immediately comply with an International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruling. The bloc framed compliance as mandatory under international law rather than optional, calling for restitution and compensation where damage is not remedied through restitution, and stated that accountability for crimes against the Rohingya was essential to a sustainable resolution of the crisis and regional stability. EU officials described the ICJ's independence and authority as more important amid threats to peace and widespread violations of international law, urging all states to respect its decisions. The statement followed the UN court's Thursday ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims in 2017 during military operations in northern Rakhine State, a decision reached by a vote of 9-6 and marking the first time the ICJ held a state responsible for genocide.
items.title: EU urges Myanmar to implement ICJ genocide ruling without delay

items.summary: Google announced Thursday that its Gemini assistant can now take control of a Mac to complete tasks for users through a feature called 'computer use,' which handles clicking, typing, menu navigation and form filling. Google cited examples such as color-grading photos in the user's design software and preparing clothing images from a folder for resale listings. The capability is available immediately for US subscribers with the Mac Gemini app on AI Plus, Pro or Ultra plans. OpenAI's ChatGPT and Meta Platforms' Muse already offer similar computer-use features in their Mac software, so Google joins existing competition rather than introducing an isolated development. When active, Gemini operates in a background window while users keep control of the main screen and cursor, can select which apps it may access, watch actions live, pause at any time and approve key steps before they occur. The feature raises pressure on Apple to make Siri more capable; current Siri handles tasks within Apple's own apps like iMessages and calendar appointments but does not extend to most third-party software, though Apple has released frameworks allowing developers to add such abilities. Apple also faces growing tension with third-party AI tools as agents adopt computer-use features, prompting the company to pledge new privacy controls on Macs after warning of rising risks from broad data access to AI software.
items.title: Google's Gemini gains computer-use control over Macs, intensifying pressure on Apple to upgrade Siri

items.summary: Anthropic began trading on Nasdaq Thursday with a stated $1.5 trillion valuation; its stock closed at $97.17, up 17 percent from the $83 IPO price. Its market value ended around $1.3 trillion by outstanding shares or $1.8 trillion fully diluted. The article frames this as reshaping venture capital toward larger bets and fatter checks, but presents that framing as opinion rather than established fact. Venture investors earned large returns: Spark Capital led a 2023 Series C at a $4.5 billion valuation; Menlo invested over $1 billion for nearly 1.5 percent of the company (worth over $20 billion at the stated market cap) and raised a separate $750 million special-purpose vehicle from limited partners, per one person familiar with the deal; Sequoia has invested $3 billion across rounds led by GIC/Coatue at $380 billion post-money in February and later co-led at $965 billion; Lightspeed holds over 2 percent as the largest financial investor after investing more than $3 billion, per two people familiar with the matter; Iconiq invested $6.1 billion to become the second-largest financial investor by ownership, according to Will Griffith of Iconiq; Amazon and Alphabet's Google together hold about 28.4 percent. The article attributes the returns to rapid valuation growth (from $61.5 billion in March 2025 to $965 billion) and revenue that it reports grew from about $1 billion at the start of 2025 to about $81 billion last month, though these figures are reported claims rather than independently verified data.
items.title: Anthropic's IPO priced at $1.5 trillion valuation

items.summary: Anthropic's first trading session ended roughly 17% higher at a $2 trillion valuation, with shares priced at $83 each. The listing converted about 5,100 of the company's ~5,300 employees (96%) into holders of equity worth over $1 million on paper; around 2,800 "Ants" hold more than $10 million and roughly 600 exceed $100 million. Andrew Benson of Hill.com attributed the speed to Anthropic's rapid expansion from under 1,000 employees at end-2024 to ~5,300 by September 2025, noting that early joining outweighs seniority for financial returns and discouraged departures. The windfall compares with SpaceX's June IPO creating about 4,400 millionaires from a larger workforce after more than two decades private; the companies also differ in geographic concentration (Anthropic concentrated in San Francisco versus SpaceX across Texas, California and Florida). A distinguishing feature was that non-founder insiders could sell up to 10% of their shares on day one rather than waiting through a typical three- to six-month lockup, though it is not known how many employees used this option.
items.title: Anthropic's IPO turned nearly its entire workforce into paper millionaires

items.summary: Meta testified before a Senate committee reviewing Bill C-22 that its proposed lawful access provisions would force technology companies to compromise digital security in order to comply with police warrants. Robyn Greene, Meta's director of privacy and public policy, told senators the government would be enforcing "a law that it is not technically feasible to comply with and still offer secure, end-to-end encrypted services to Canadians." When pressed about withdrawing products if the bill became law, Rachel Curran, Meta's head of public policy for Canada, said the company would have to "review all of our options," echoing a Bloomberg statement in which she called weakening encryption a "red line" and warned the legislation risks turning private companies into "an arm of the government's surveillance apparatus." The standoff centers on Part 2 of Bill C-22, which passed the House of Commons in June but had not yet been enacted. That part grants ministers authority to issue confidential orders compelling service providers to build law enforcement access capabilities and permits requiring retention of customer metadata for up to six months. Ottawa's amendments barring orders that create a "systemic vulnerability" are contested by tech leaders and cryptographers, who argue the language is too vague; security experts maintain that building a backdoor for police inevitably exposes the same entry point to cybercriminals and foreign intelligence agencies. Meta joins Google, Apple, Signal, and Windscribe in opposing or responding to the draft law, though their positions differ: both Google and Apple warned of threats to customer security, Signal said it would leave Canada rather than compromise its protocols, and Windscribe pledged to maintain its no-logs policy regardless of the bill's outcome. These are reported statements from company representatives about a not-yet-enacted measure; Meta has framed withdrawal as something it may "consider" or must "review," not a confirmed decision.
items.title: Meta warns it may withdraw encrypted services from Canada over Bill C-22

items.summary: Anthropic's initial public offering on Wednesday added another marquee tech listing to Nasdaq, which displayed the debut where more than 800 million shares changed hands. According to Dealogic data through this year, Nasdaq hosted 64 IPOs led by Anthropic and SpaceX raising about $201.8 billion versus NYSE's 42 deals raising $20.8 billion, described as the widest capital-raising gap since tracking began in 1995; these figures are attributed to Dealogic rather than established fact. Nasdaq finished ahead of NYSE six out of eight times between 2018 and 2025 per Dealogic, though that is a reported record through this year's projection. Nasdaq CEO Adena Friedman cited the exchange's IPO marketing strength, its investor-relations business connecting companies with large asset managers, and its index business launched in 1985 as competitive advantages; her quotes are attributed to her interview on Thursday. Analyst Owen Lau of Clear Street said NYSE faces a hard problem because Nasdaq built its private markets business and indexes years earlier, suggesting NYSE may need to copy those moves over the past decade; his views are attributed to him but represent opinion rather than fact. The article reports that two people familiar with the matter say NYSE executives face increasing pressure to win the next mega-IPO after recent losses, while NYSE declined to comment.
items.title: Nasdaq's IPO market-share lead over NYSE widens to a record after Anthropic listing

items.summary: Anthropic shares began trading on Nasdaq at $111.50, 34% above its IPO price of $83 per share set Wednesday evening for early shareholders; the company priced this above its initially indicated range of $70-$78 and expanded shares offered from 833 million to 980 million. In the first ten minutes trading reached a market valuation of $2.09 trillion, surpassing SpaceX's listing, before paring gains to close at $97.17, or 17.07% above IPO price; the expanded share count raised its final valuation to $1.5 trillion. The higher-than-expected pricing occurred despite investor concerns following Jensen Huang's ouster from Nvidia amid a potential Chinese espionage scandal and cooling AI enthusiasm. Michael Rosen of Angeles Investments said strong demand gave a near-term sentiment boost but reflected a realignment favoring hyperscalers over pure data-center buildout exposure; Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co called it a big win for tech showing strong investor demand; Ben Reitzes of Melius Research opened with a buy rating and $155 price target, implying roughly 87% upside from IPO price. Brokerages expect revenues around $400 million by 2029, with more than 20 banks involved in the deal led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley.
items.title: Anthropic IPO debut and pricing

items.summary: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi criticized Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday following a trilateral summit between the United States, Russia and China held in Shenzhen on November 19. The meeting produced a joint declaration titled 'The Russia-China-US Heads of State Declaration Toward Peace,' which featured Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. This report is based on Rahul Gandhi's statements as reported by The Times of India; his specific characterization of Modi—described here only in the headline—is attributed to him rather than presented as established fact.
items.title: Rahul Gandhi criticizes Modi after US-Russia-China summit

items.summary: A survey of 193 Asia-Pacific fund managers overseeing $526 billion, conducted between November 6 and 12 with 94 respondents ($241 billion) participating in regional questions, found India's net overweight position at 5% in November, matching South Korea. Japan led the region at a 38% net overweight, followed by Taiwan at 24%, while Indonesia was least favoured at a 33% net underweight. The survey attributed the shift toward India to growing caution about AI-centric markets like South Korea and Taiwan, with respondents citing deteriorating growth and corporate profit expectations possibly reflecting interest rate concerns and drawdowns in AI-related stocks; one quote stated investors are increasingly rotating out of AI and into defensives. About 29% of respondents cited the absence of a major AI investment opportunity as their biggest concern about Indian equities, up from 25% in October.
items.title: India becomes net overweight among Asia-Pacific fund managers after 10 months

items.summary: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi responded to being called a 'youth leader' despite his age during a conversation at the University of Chicago, arguing that remaining curious and asking questions across all subjects is what keeps people young. He said he was taught from childhood never to place boundaries on curiosity, encouraging inquiry about geopolitics, women's health, animals, and other topics, while observing that society gradually restricts adults' questioning as they age toward conventional measures of success like earning money or owning property. Gandhi framed this refusal to accept such limits as the essence of youth, suggesting it explains why others call him a 'youth leader.' He added that he never accepted questions should be off-limits and cited his former mathematics tutor pursuing a master's degree in his 60s as an example. The conversation also turned to generational change in Western political leadership, where Gandhi claimed leaders early in his career had broader global understanding than those who later focused inward on domestic issues; he attributed this shift partly to younger American leaders now reengaging with international affairs and praised Vladimir Putin's geopolitical breadth while noting the trend was an experience rather than a verified fact. All claims are Rahul Gandhi's own views expressed at the University of Chicago conversation, not established facts.
items.title: Rahul Gandhi defends 'youth leader' label at 56, citing curiosity as defining youth

items.summary: On November 20, Brent crude futures gained 54 cents or 0.55% to settle at $92.60 a barrel; WTI December climbed 32 cents or 0.38% to $83.53 and the January contract rose 20 cents or 0.2% to $82.64, yet both benchmarks headed for a third consecutive weekly decline as recovering crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz strengthened expectations of a global supply surplus. The Iran-aligned Houthis fired missiles at Riyadh on that day, renewing concerns over regional oil security, and reports cited by Reuters from Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said two tankers hit naval mines in the waterway and exploded or were burning. A separate claim attributed to an unspecified source states global oil demand could fall by more than 4% by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, improve energy efficiency, and switch to alternative fuels. Goldman Sachs raised its projections earlier that month, forecasting Brent at $140 in 2027 if Gulf production stays significantly below its 2025 average; it lifted its December Brent forecast to $105 from $90 and WTI to $94 from $81, with a bullish scenario putting Brent near $140 or averaging about $130 in 2027 if Gulf output stays roughly 3.5 million barrels per day below the 2025 average; these are forecasts, not outcomes. JPMorgan's base case assumes Middle Eastern supplies will exceed their 2025 average via ship-to-ship transfers and additional pipeline capacity while production growth elsewhere halts. The article carries a disclaimer that its author is not a SEBI-registered research analyst or investment adviser.
items.title: Brent crude rose 0.55% to $92.60 on November 20, marking a third consecutive weekly decline

items.summary: A new book, Counting a Nation by C Chandramouli (Pan Macmillan India), argues that Census 2027 must serve as an act of statistical recovery rather than routine enumeration. The author contends the Covid-19 pandemic disrupted India's Civil Registration System, which records births and deaths, leaving rural mortality underreported while independent studies suggested excess mortality above official figures; lockdowns also delayed tabulation and strained states' ability to transmit data centrally. Because census projections normally extend from a 2011 baseline using registered vital statistics, the compromised CRS left population estimates for 2020-25 fragile and made urbanisation figures unreliable as migrant workers returned to villages during lockdowns with unknown subsequent returns. Chandramouli asserts that large-scale sample surveys including the NSS, NFHS, PLFS, and household consumption or employment surveys depend on the census frame built during houselisting, so the decade-old 2011 frame now risks coverage error as new towns emerge, migration reshapes densities, villages depopulate, and peri-urban areas expand. The author frames a sixteen-year gap between censuses as fracturing India's time series continuity that has existed since 1881, complicating demographic analysis, economic planning, international comparisons at the UN and World Bank, and electoral studies for delimitation; he notes one option is to regress 2027 data backwards using projections and sample surveys but warns this yields approximations rather than authoritative benchmarks. Chandramouli states Census 2027 must rebuild the master sampling frame underpinning every major survey and restore credibility, while acknowledging these are claims from an excerpted book account rather than established outcomes.
items.title: Census 2027 framed as essential statistical recovery for India after pandemic disruptions

items.summary: According to monitoring data from AQI.in, Delhi recorded an Air Quality Index of 510 at 7:11 AM on Friday, November 20, placing the city in the hazardous category after overnight pollution rose sharply and reversed Thursday afternoon's improvement. PM2.5 reached 330 micrograms per cubic metre and PM10 reached 462 micrograms per cubic metre; carbon monoxide stood at 2,066 parts per billion, with nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide and ozone measured at 22, six and two parts per billion respectively. The platform's historical data attributes the morning spike to a peak of 563 on November 19 before afternoon decline to 178; AQI.in estimates that breathing Delhi's air equates to smoking 10.2 cigarettes daily (71.4 weekly, 306 monthly). AQI.in advises staying indoors and wearing N95 masks as a must, plus using air purifiers and car filters. The November trend is described by the platform as worsening overall: an AQI of 666 on November 9 fell to 224 on November 17 before rising again to 273 on November 18 and 353 on November 19, with Delhi ranking eighth among the world's most polluted cities. The article attributes these figures solely to AQI.in as an unverified source; it does not independently confirm them.
items.title: Delhi AQI hit 510 (hazardous) on November 20, per AQI.in

items.summary: At a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen on APEC sidelines, Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin issued a joint statement reaffirming that "a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought," echoing the Reagan-Gorbachev principle first formalized after their 1985 Geneva summit. The leaders agreed to dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation but set no timeline for those talks, offered no concrete commitment to cut arsenals, and made no mention of a trilateral arms-reduction agreement Trump has advocated since his first term. China's reluctance stems from its considerably smaller arsenal; SIPRI estimates put it at 620 warheads in January 2026 versus 5,420 for Russia and 5,042 for the US. The declaration is widely characterized as a reiteration of an established principle rather than new diplomacy, with no immediate diplomatic progress beyond restating the shared understanding.
items.title: Trump, Xi and Putin reaffirmed an existing nuclear-war pledge without committing to arms reduction

items.summary: The author, reflecting on growing up in India during the mid-2000s to 2010s Harry Potter and Twilight fandoms, recounts how Robert Pattinson became a teenage heartthrob after playing Cedric Diggory for about two minutes in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (2005), then again as Edward Cullen in the Twilight film adaptation. The author notes that Team Jacob vs Team Edward rivalries over Taylor Lautner reflected college-era crushes, and describes how Pattinson later worked to avoid typecasting before being announced as James Bond on November 16; the author states their first reaction was that 'Team Edward had won,' while also musing that an actor who rose through female-oriented wish-fulfilment fantasy would now play what they call the ultimate male fantasy. The account is a personal memoir and contains no reported figures, quotes with attribution, or forecasts to verify.
items.title: A former Twilight heartthrob cast as James Bond

items.summary: The District Crime Branch searched former Tamil Nadu Minister Murthy's residence as part of a quarrying investigation, filing a case citing alleged illegal excavation of red soil and stone from various quarries during his tenure. The probe follows an FIR against DMK leader Durai Murugan for illegal sand excavation. Officials are reviewing documents to identify environmental violations and secure evidence.
items.title: Police search former Tamil Nadu Minister Murthy's home over quarrying irregularities case

items.summary: The 57th International Film Festival of India in Goa (November 20-28) will screen fourteen films that won prizes at this year's Cannes, Berlin and Venice festivals: seven from Cannes, three from Berlin and four from Venice. Paweł Pawlikowski's 'Fatherland', which shared the Best Director prize at Cannes, opens the festival; May el-Toukhy's Golden Lion winner 'Woman Unknown' is among the Venice entries. However, several of the year's biggest winners are absent: Cristian Mungiu's Palme d'Or-winning 'Fjord', İlker Çatak's Golden Bear winner 'Yellow Letters', Andrey Zvyagintsev's Grand Prix film 'Minotaur', Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo's Camera d'Or winner 'Ben'Imana', Markus Schleinzer's Berlin Silver Bear for Best Leading Performance 'Rose', and Venice entries including Lee Chang-dong's 'Possible Love', Ilya Khrzhanovsky's 'DAU', and Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor's 'NAZA'. Notably, none of the 12 international films competing for IFFI's Golden Peacock won a major award at Cannes, Berlin or Venice. Organisers received more than 1,900 submissions from 137 countries; festival director is Ashutosh Gowariker. Hindustan Times contacted NFDC to ask why these films are excluded but had not received a response as of the report's filing, and said it would update if one came in.
items.title: IFFI 2026 schedule includes Cannes, Berlin and Venice prize winners but omits several top laureates

items.summary: The BJP has launched a political campaign themed around Grand Theft Auto (GTA) targeting Tamil Nadu Chief Minister M.K. Stalin, whom the item calls 'Vijay,' focusing on law and order issues; this follows similar moves by the opposition. The text attributes these actions to party actors without further detail or evidence of effectiveness.
items.title: BJP launches GTA-themed campaign against Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay over law and order

items.summary: A Supreme Court bench of justices N Kotiswar Singh and NV Anjaria ruled that an unwed mother has a stronger prima facie claim to custody of her minor child, directing the father—a lawyer running a firm with around 53 associates—to hand over interim custody of their four-year-old son to his German-based mother in Singapore. The court held this preferential position cannot be negated by the absence of marriage or any particular statute, while clarifying it does not exclude the father's claim but establishes only her better prima facie standing; no legal provision disables a young mother from such a claim. On welfare grounds, both parents were found equally capable and free of diagnosable psychiatric disorders, yet the court judged the mother's proposal more beneficial because she had made concrete schooling arrangements in Singapore and could adjust her work schedule, whereas the father would likely depend on relatives and nannies given his demanding practice; it expressed doubt that he could spare adequate time for an energetic four-year-old. A NIMHANS report found the child had been out of formal schooling for about four months with resulting behavioural difficulties and recommended resuming classes promptly, while noting the boy's fluency in German and English reflected a closer bond with his mother; the court rejected the father's argument that relocation would uproot him, observing stability comes from people and routines rather than geography. The decision is confined to interim custody: the mother must obtain a mirror order from a competent Singapore court within three weeks, deposit ₹1 crore, grant daily video access of at least 20 minutes plus visitation in Singapore and custody during visits to India, and bring the child back for school vacations exceeding seven days; the Family Court at Delhi will independently decide permanent guardianship. The article is reporting by Utkarsh Anand of Hindustan Times.
items.title: Supreme Court gives unwed mother a better prima facie claim to custody of her child

items.summary: Delhi Police and Noida STF officials said on Friday that gangster Naseem Durrani was killed during a joint police operation in Bulandshahr. He had been suspected of involvement in the November 16 shooting death of Sameer outside Delhi law minister Kapil Mishra's camp office in Sonia Vihar, northeast Delhi; investigators reported around 16 rounds were fired at the victim. Durrani reportedly has about 25 criminal cases against him and was linked to underworld operative Chhota Shakeel. The claim that he was killed is attributed only to police officials.
items.title: Gangster Naseem Durrani killed in joint police operation in Bulandshahr

items.summary: A car caught fire shortly after ramming a lorry from behind in the early hours of Friday on the Kokapet Outer Ring Road (ORR) near Hyderabad. The vehicle was travelling from Shamshabad toward Kokapet and carried two people at the time, all of whom survived with no casualties reported. Police reached the scene to investigate and registered a case; further details were pending as of report.
items.title: Car catches fire after rear-ending lorry on Kokapet ORR; no casualties reported

items.summary: The foreign ministers of Jordan, the UAE, Indonesia, Pakistan, Türkiye, Algeria, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Oman, Palestine, Qatar, Kuwait, Libya, Maldives, Egypt and Niger issued a joint statement welcoming the United Kingdom's and Australia's decisions to impose sanctions over Israeli settlement activities in the occupied West Bank. The declaration calls for greater accountability against entities and individuals involved in settlement expansion and annexation policies, including what it terms the E1 settlement plan east of occupied East Jerusalem. It also welcomed the UK sanctioning an organisation accused of obstructing humanitarian aid to Gaza. The ministers described the measures as consistent with international law and UN Security Council Resolution 2334 (2016) and the International Court of Justice's July 19, 2024 advisory opinion, reiterated calls for Israel to rescind settlement-related measures, condemned Israeli military escalation in Gaza, endorsed Trump's Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict, and affirmed support for a two-State solution based on the June 4, 1967 lines with East Jerusalem as capital. The statement is an agency feed not edited by FPJ's editorial team.
items.title: Fifteen Arab and Islamic nations welcome UK and Australia sanctions on Israeli West Bank settlements

items.summary: Indian fast bowler Jasprit Bumrah took four wickets in 29 overs during the first Test versus New Zealand. The article presents several of his statements as reflections on mindset: that concentrating on one ball at a time reduces pressure; that success requires work rather than talent alone, since nothing comes easy; that focusing on process instead of chasing results is key to goals; and that clarity about plans improves execution. These quotes are offered by the source as illustrations of Bumrah's approach, with the article drawing inferences—such as claims that his focus 'helps manage pressure' or makes him 'act with confidence'—that extend beyond what he literally said.
items.title: Jasprit Bumrah quotes on focus and process, framed around a four-wicket Test performance against New Zealand

items.summary: Police officials say gangster Naseem Durrani was killed during a joint operation by the Delhi Police and Noida Special Task Force (STF) that broke out into an encounter in Bulandshahr, Uttar Pradesh. He had been tracked after police received intelligence about his presence there following the November 16 shooting of Sameer outside the office of Delhi Law Minister Kapil Mishra; armed assailants reportedly fired around 20 rounds at Sameer before he died at a hospital. Durrani is alleged to be linked to Dawood Ibrahim's D-Company and Chhota Shakeel, who reportedly assigned him in 2016 to kill jailed gangster Chhota Rajan, and is also accused of plotting the assassination of journalist Tarek Fatah; he faced more than 25 criminal cases. The killing comes amid an investigation into Sameer's murder, which was suspected to stem from a rivalry between Durrani and Haroon Saifi gangs, though Sameer had reportedly been detained for questioning in another case before being released. Further details on the encounter, exchange of fire, and Durrani's alleged role remain awaited.
items.title: Naseem Durrani killed in Delhi Police-Noida STF encounter in Bulandshahr, UP
